reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of histidase (histidine ammonia-lyase, HAL), the first enzyme of histidine degradation that converts histidine to urocanic acid

Now regarded as an essentially benign biochemical condition; historical associations with speech delay and intellectual disability were largely ascription artefacts of the era before newborn screening controls
The biochemical signature is raised plasma and urine histidine with reduced or absent urinary urocanic acid, and elevated histidine metabolites (imidazole compounds) in urine
Most individuals detected through screening are healthy and require no treatment
A sweat/skin test showing absent urocanic acid supports the diagnosis, as urocanic acid is normally abundant in skin and sweat
It is important not to attribute unrelated developmental problems to the biochemical finding
Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and dietary histidine restriction is not warranted for the benign condition
reference.pathophysiology: Histidine is normally degraded by histidase, which removes ammonia to form urocanic acid en route to glutamate formation. In histidinaemia, deficient histidase activity causes histidine to accumulate in plasma and urine while urocanic acid, normally produced in liver and skin, is reduced or absent. Because the accumulated histidine and its transamination products (imidazole derivatives) are not appreciably toxic, the condition is now considered a benign inborn variation of metabolism rather than a cause of neurological disease.
additionalDifferentials: Other benign aminoacidaemias identified on newborn screening
Secondary histidine elevation from folate status or dietary factors
Urea cycle or transport disorders with altered amino acid profiles
Coincidental neurodevelopmental disorder of separate cause
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma amino acids showing elevated histidine
Urine amino acids and imidazole metabolites with absent/low urocanic acid
Skin or sweat urocanic acid testing
Histidase enzyme assay (historically in stratum corneum or liver) where confirmation is sought
Molecular analysis of the HAL gene
Evaluation for an alternative diagnosis if symptoms are present
redFlags: Attributing significant developmental or neurological problems to histidinaemia without other evaluation
Progressive symptoms suggesting a different, coexisting disorder
Unnecessary dietary restriction causing nutritional compromise
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent, as histidinaemia is now recognised as a benign metabolic trait with normal development expected in the great majority. No treatment is generally required.
pitfalls: Treating a benign biochemical finding as a disease requiring dietary therapy
Falsely linking developmental delay to the histidine elevation
Confusing it with a more serious aminoacidopathy
Missing a separate primary diagnosis when symptoms coexist
